summary: Discusses and formalizes channel binding: tying authentication done at a higher layer to the secure channel set up at a lower layer, so both sides know they are the same endpoints. This lets applications rely on lower-layer protection while still getting the assurance they need. It also describes the pros, cons and security considerations.

plainLanguage.summary: Channel binding checks that the peer authenticated by an application is connected to the same secure channel used underneath it. This can let an application rely on lower-layer protection without accepting a hidden intermediary.

subtitle: Channel binding connects application authentication to a lower secure channel.

tldr.problem: Application authentication and lower-layer encryption may identify different peers, allowing a man-in-the-middle between the layers.
tldr.mechanism: Both endpoints compare data naming the lower secure channel or its authenticated endpoints during higher-layer authentication.
tldr.outcome: Applications can delegate some session protection to lower layers while checking that authentication and channel endpoints match.

today: RFC 5056 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2007. The work-unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Bind Two Security Layers
sections.content:
An application may authenticate a user while relying on IPsec or another lower network layer to protect the connection. Without a link between these layers, a man-in-the-middle could be present from the application's point of view.

RFC 5056 formalizes channel binding as a way to connect higher-layer authentication to a lower secure channel. It generalizes the GSS-API concept for use with other authentication frameworks and protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: An application may verify a user while another layer protects the connection. Channel binding checks that both layers refer to the same endpoints.

sections.title: Unique and Endpoint Bindings
sections.content:
A secure channel provides cryptographic integrity and may provide confidentiality. Channel bindings are data that name a channel or its endpoints so both sides can compare them at the application layer.

A unique binding identifies one channel in a cryptographically secure way. An endpoint binding identifies one or both authenticated endpoints, but does not uniquely identify a channel in time.
sections.plainLanguage: A binding is information about a secure connection that both endpoints can compare. Some bindings identify one particular connection; others identify its endpoint or endpoints.

sections.title: Requirements for Using Bindings
sections.content:
An application MUST check that both endpoints observe the same channel bindings and authenticate at least one application peer. If the authentication method supports channel binding, the application SHOULD use it; otherwise, the application must exchange the bindings through an integrity-protected method.

Specifications define one canonical encoding and the binding type. The application MUST NOT send sensitive data before binding completes, and revealing the binding MUST NOT weaken the channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must compare the same binding data through an authenticated, integrity-protected exchange. They wait for that check to succeed before sending sensitive information.

sections.title: Authentication Frameworks
sections.content:
The GSS-API supports channel binding during security-context setup, but mechanisms are not required to implement it. A GSS-API mechanism fails context establishment if the binding fails, so applications must agree in advance whether to use it.

At publication, SASL work to add channel-binding support was still in progress. When a framework lacks a suitable feature, an application protocol may exchange bindings separately using at least integrity protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Some authentication systems have a built-in place to check a channel binding, and others do not. An application can use a protected exchange when its framework lacks that feature.

sections.title: Examples for SSH and TLS
sections.content:
The RFC gives non-normative examples. For SSHv2, the session ID can serve as a unique binding because it covers key exchange and negotiation. A TLS session ID is not suitable: the server assigns it, so a man-in-the-middle can assign the same value.

For TLS, the initial Finished messages can serve as unique bindings because they are keyed outputs over the handshake. SSH host public keys and TLS server certificates can be endpoint bindings when the negotiated method actually uses them.
sections.plainLanguage: A useful binding must be tied to the secure setup, not merely chosen by a server. The RFC's examples use handshake-derived values for unique channel bindings.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Delegating protection between layers may trade one layer's cryptographic strength for another's. Security depends on the channel, how bindings are constructed, and the application's authentication method.

Non-unique bindings can create risks on systems that serve multiple users. The RFC's NFS example warns that another user might reuse channel bindings to impersonate authenticated users unless the server requires fresh authentication or uses sufficiently protected, hard-to-guess values.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel binding does not make a weak channel strong. Applications must choose a suitable channel and prevent one user's binding data from being reused as another user's identity.
